html:
The Battle of Tondibi was fought in March 1591 near Gao, on the Niger in today's Mali. A Moroccan army with firearms crushed the much larger army of the Songhai Empire, the greatest state of West Africa, and the empire fell apart.

Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur of Morocco's Saadi dynasty wanted the gold of West Africa. He sent a few thousand soldiers, many of them Andalusian exiles and European converts, across the Sahara under Judar Pasha, a long march that killed many of them. At Tondibi the Songhai king Askia Ishaq II drove a herd of cattle at the enemy, but the gunfire scattered the animals and the Songhai lines broke.

The Moroccans took Gao and Timbuktu and exiled many of its scholars. They never found the gold mines, which lay further south. Their soldiers settled as a ruling caste, the Arma, but lost touch with Morocco. With no great state to hold it together, the middle Niger split into smaller powers.
